newsitem.title: GERMANY: East German women cook up surprise for soldiers.
newsitem.headline: East German women cook up surprise for soldiers.

text.p: The mothers and grandmothers of this usually idyllic east German village cooked up an idea on Sunday to thank the army troops who have defended their homes and farms against looming flood waters.

Ovens across town glowed through the night as the women of Hohenwutzen baked cakes to help boost morale among the hundreds of soldiers who have been working 12-hour shifts every day to fortify the dikes.

A tenacious 64-year-old grandmother organised the cake campaign. Beginning Saturday morning, Hildegard Obitz started a telephone campaign to arrange a shipment of baked goods and coffee for a Sunday afternoon break from disaster prevention.

"It's going to be a surprise," Obitz said with a grin, as she lowered the third sheet of sugar and cocoa sheet cakes into her oven. "I just felt like it was time we say thank you for everything those boys are doing out there on the dikes."
Hohenwutzen is under normal conditions a waterfront resort village with well-kept yards, blooming gardens and family-owned inns.

But since the River Oder began to creep higher and dams began to sag, there have been more soldiers than local residents in town and helicopters whir overhead, bringing tonnes of sand and gravel to reinforce the weakening dikes.
Many of the local men have pitched in, either by filling sandbags or driving flatbed trucks full of sand to the spots along the dike where soldiers were furiously repairing cracks.

But now women like Obitz and her neighbours Magdalena Schroeder, 63, and Anita Fehlmaelcher, 64, want to bring a bit of small town hospitality to the muddy fields where the soldiers have been working, and often sleeping.
The women say such community projects are a tradition in small German towns, particularly in the former communist east.

"Those of us who spent 40 years in East Germany never had it as good as those in the west," Schroeder said over an apple cake in the making. "We learned how to help one another because we had to, and that is just what we are doing now."
Schroeder and her husband have been evacuated from their home and are living on her sister-in-law's chicken farm until the floods pass.
"To be honest, I don't know what we'll do if the dams break and we return home to nothing," Schroeder said.

"I remember the flood of 1947 and this is worse in so many ways," she said. "At that time, it was just after the war, we had run from the Russian army and we were dirt poor. We didn't have that much to lose.
"Now we've built something here and I know we would have already lost everything if the army hadn't come."
Fehlmaelcher nodded. "Maybe all these sweets will let the soldiers out there know that they're doing something worthwhile for us and we're grateful," she said.
